title: Delhi Nagrik Sehkari Bank vs Chander Pal on 11 March, 2022
full_text: Delhi Nagrik Sehkari Bank vs Chander Pal on 11 March, 2022 CC No. 629035/2016 Delhi Nagrik Sehkari Bank vs Chander Pal IN THE COURT OF MS. TWINKLE CHAWLA: MM, NI ACT-02, SOUTH- EAST DISTRICT, SAKET COURTS COMPLEX: NEW DELHI Delhi Nagrik Sehkari Bank vs Chander Pal CC No. 629035/2016 U/s 138 Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 1. CIS number : DLSE020099332015 2. Name of the Complainant : Delhi Nagrik Sehkari Bank 3. Name of the Accused, : Sh. Chander Pal, s/o Lt. Sh. Mohan Pal parentage & residential address R/o G-12/221, Sangam Vihar, near Noorani Masjid, New Delhi. 4. Offence complained of or : U/s 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act , proved 1881 5. Plea of the Accused : Pleaded not guilty and claimed trial 6. Final Judgment/order : CONVICTED 7. Date of judgment/order : 11.03.2022 JUDGMENT 1. Complainant has filed the present complaint under Section 138 / 142 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (" NI Act ") on the averments that, being a 1|Page CC No. 629035/2016 Delhi Nagrik Sehkari Bank vs Chander Pal cooperative bank, the Complainant had extended a loan of Rs. 5,00,000/- to the Accused, who was a member of the said Complainant bank, bearing membership no. 91092. 2. In part payment of the loan, the Accused is stated to have issued a cheque bearing No. 479365 dt. 10.08.2015 drawn on Syndicate Bank, Dr. Ambedkar Nagar, DTC Depot, New Delhi-110062, for an amount of Rs. 4,00,000/-, in favour of the Complainant (hereinafter referred as "cheque in question"). 3. However, when the Complainant presented the cheque in question; the same was returned unpaid vide return memo dated 21.09.2015, for the reason "funds insufficient". The Complainant sent the legal demand notice dated 20.10.2015 through their counsel by speed post at the registered address of the Accused. Hence, despite the service of the legal demand notice, the Accused failed to reply to the legal demand notice and make the payment and hence, the Complainant filed the present complaint. 4. The AR of the Complainant bank examined himself as CW1 and tendered his pre summoning evidence affidavit Ex. CW1/B and also proved following documents: Ex. CW1/1: Copy of the General Power of Attorney dt. 12.01.2011 along with board resolution dt. 23.12.2010. Ex CW1/2: Letter of authority in favour of the AR. 2|Page CC No. 629035/2016 Delhi Nagrik Sehkari Bank vs Chander Pal Ex. CW1/3: Cheque bearing no. 479365 of Rs. 4,00,000/- in favour of the Complainant bank. Ex. CW1/4: Return memo dt. 21.09.2015 on grounds of funds insufficient. Ex. CW1/5: Legal demand notice dt. 20.10.2015 Ex. CW1/6: Postal receipt dt. 21.10.2015 in respect of the legal demand notice. Ex. CW1/A: Complaint u/s 138 NI Act. 5. After taking pre-summoning evidence, Accused was ordered to be summoned in this case for commission of offence under Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (" NI Act "), vide order dated 08.12.2015. 6. Accused appeared and was released on bail on 19.04.2016. On finding a prima facie case, notice U/s 251 of the Criminal Procedure Code , 1973 (" CrPC ") was served upon the Accused on 02.07.2016 to which he pleaded not guilty and opted to contest after disclosing the following defence: "I do not plead guilty and claim trial. I had taken loan of Rs. 5 lacs from the complainant. As security, I had issued three blank signed cheques to the complainant. I had not received any legal demand notice. I have already repaid Rs. 2 lacs." 7. Vide order dated 05.08.2016, opportunity was granted to the complainant to cross examine the Accused. However, right to cross-examine the Complainant was closed by court order dt. 28.02.2019. 3|Page CC No. 629035/2016 Delhi Nagrik Sehkari Bank vs Chander Pal 8. Thereafter, Accused was examined under Section 313 of CrPC for explaining the circumstances appearing against him in the Complainant's evidence. He denied the Complainant's case and pleaded false implication in the present case and opted to lead evidence in his defence. 9. Accused examined himself as DW1 and one Ms. Vandana Aggarwal, Clerk cum Cashier at Delhi Nagrik Sehkari Bank as DW2, who proved the following document: Ex. Account statement of Accused from DW2/X 05.04.2011 to 30.09.2021. 10.Defence evidence was closed vide separate statement of the Accused on 29.11.2021. 11.I have heard Ld. Counsel for the parties and have perused the case file carefully and meticulously. Submissions of the Complainant and Accused 12.Complainant has submitted that all ingredients of Section 138 NI Act are fulfilled in the present case and hence, the presumption under Section 139 NI Act arises in the favour of the Complainant, which has not been successfully rebutted by the Accused. 13.Per contra, Ld. Counsel for the Accused has submitted that the Accused 4|Page CC No. 629035/2016 Delhi Nagrik Sehkari Bank vs Chander Pal deserves to be acquitted as the cheque in question was given as a blank signed security cheque for the loan amount of Rs. 5,00,000 and he has repaid a part of the loan. Hence, the presumption under Section 139 NI Act stands rebutted. Legal Framework Ingredients of Section 138 NI Act: 14.The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in Kusum Ingots & Alloys Ltd and Ors v. K Pennar Peterson Securities Ltd and Ors. , (2000) 2 SCC 745 ("Kusum Ingots Case"), has clearly stipulated that "the ingredients which are to be satisfied for making out a case under the provision are: (i) a person must have drawn a cheque on an account maintained by him in a bank for payment of a certain amount of money to another person from out of that account for the discharge of any debt or other liability; (ii) that cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months1 from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity whichever is earlier; (iii) that cheque is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of the account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that 1 Reduced to three months vide RBI circular dated 4.11.2011. 5|Page CC No. 629035/2016 Delhi Nagrik Sehkari Bank vs Chander Pal account by an agreement made with the bank; (iv) the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque makes a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice in writing, to the drawer of the cheque, within 152 days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid; and (v) the drawer of such cheque fails to make payment of the said amount of money to the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque within 15 days of the receipt of the said notice; If the aforementioned ingredients are satisfied then the person who has drawn the cheque shall be deemed to have committed an offence." 15.Therefore, if the aforesaid ingredients are made out, the Accused is deemed to have committed an offence under Section 138 NI Act. Presumption under Section 139 NI Act/ Section 118 NI Act: 16. Section 139 NI Act states that: "Presumption in favour of holder: It shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque of 2 The same is now enhanced to 30 days. 6|Page CC No. 629035/2016 Delhi Nagrik Sehkari Bank vs Chander Pal the nature referred to in section 138 for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability" 17. Section 139 NI Act is a type of reverse onus clause, which stipulates a presumption in the favour of the Complainant as to fact of a cheque being received in discharge of a legal debt or liability. 18.Further, Section 118(a) of the NI Act, states as follows: "Presumptions as to negotiable instruments. -- Until the contrary is proved, the following presumptions shall be made: a of consideration --that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration, and that every such instrument, when it has been accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred, was accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration;" 19.The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India has in a number of judgments dealt with the combined effect of the presumptions raised under Section 139 and Section 118(a) NI Act. 20.The following proposition can be summarized on a perusal of the judgments of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in Sunil Todi & Ors v. State of Gujarat, LL 2021 SC 706 ("Sunil Todi Case"); Kalamani Tex v. P. Balasubramanian , 2021 SCC OnLine SC 75; APS Forex Services Pvt. Ltd. v. Shakti International 7|Page CC No. 629035/2016 Delhi Nagrik Sehkari Bank vs Chander Pal Fashion Linkers and Ors., AIR 2020 SC 945; Rohitbhai Jivanlal Patel v. State of Gujarat and Ors., AIR 2019 SC 1876; Kumar Exports v. Sharma Carpets , (2009) 2 SCC 513; Basalingappa v. Mudibasappa , (2019) 5 SCC 418; (" Basalingappa Case"); K.N. Beena v. Muniyappan and Anr. , (2001) 8 SCC 458; and Dhanvantrai Balwantrai Desai v. State of Maharashtra , 1964 Cri. LJ 437: (i) Once the execution of cheque is admitted; Section 139 of the NI Act mandates a presumption that the cheque was for the discharge of legally enforceable debt or liability; (ii) The presumption under Section 139 is a rebuttable presumption and the onus is on the Accused to raise the probable defence. The standard of proof for rebutting the presumption is that of preponderance of probabilities; (iii) Something which is probable has to be brought on record by the Accused for getting the burden of proof shifted to the Complainant. To disprove the presumptions, the Accused should bring on record such facts and circumstances, upon consideration of which, the court may either believe that the consideration and debt did not exist or their non-existence was so probable that a prudent man would under the circumstances of the case, act upon the plea that they did not exist; 8|Page CC No. 629035/2016 Delhi Nagrik Sehkari Bank vs Chander Pal (iv) The words "unless the contrary is proved" which occur in Section 139 , make it clear that the presumption has to be rebutted by 'proof' and not by a bare explanation which is merely plausible. A fact is said to be proved when its existence is directly established or when upon the material before it the Court finds its existence to be so probable that a reasonable man would act on the supposition that it exists. Unless, therefore, the explanation is supported by proof, the presumption created by Section 139 NI Act cannot be said to be rebutted; (v) To rebut the presumption, it is open for the Accused to rely on evidence led by him or the Accused can also rely on the materials submitted by the Complainant in order to raise a probable defence. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by the parties but also by reference to the circumstances upon which they rely; (vi) That it is not necessary for the Accused to come in the witness box in support of his defence, Section 139 imposed an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden. Analysis 21.In the case at hand, it is not in dispute that the cheque in question was drawn by the Accused from his bank account. Further, it is also not in dispute that the 9|Page CC No. 629035/2016 Delhi Nagrik Sehkari Bank vs Chander Pal Accused is the signatory of the cheque in question as in the defence disclosed by the Accused U/s 251 CrPC and Section 313 CrPC statement; he has duly admitted the same. Presentation of the cheque in question by the Complainant is also not in dispute. 22.The dishonour of the cheque in question by way of the return memo, Ex. CW1/4, on grounds of Funds Insufficient, is also not in dispute as the same has been admitted by the Accused in his statement u/s 313 CrPC. 23.The Complainant sent the legal demand notice, dated 20.10.2015 (Ex. CW1/5) by way of speed post (Ex. CW1/6). However, the Accused has disputed the receipt of the legal demand notice. While the Accused has disputed the receipt of the legal demand notice; it is noted that the address mentioned on the legal demand notice is same as the address mentioned by the Accused on his bail bond furnished to this Court; and the Accused has also appeared in Court pursuant to service of summons at the same address as the one mentioned in the legal demand notice. Accordingly, a presumption of due service is drawn u/s 27 of General Clauses Act which provides that where the notice is sent to the correct address of the recipient, the same shall be presumed to have been duly served. Further, the Hon'ble SC in C.C. Alavi Hazi v. Palapetty Muhammad & Anr , (2007) 6SCC 555 has held that: "Any drawer who claims that he did not receive the notice by post, can, within 15 days of receipt of summons from the court in respect of the 10 | P a g e CC No. 629035/2016 Delhi Nagrik Sehkari Bank vs Chander Pal complaint U/s 138 of the Act, make payment of the cheque amount and submit to the court that he had made payment within 15 days of receipt of summons (by receiving a copy of complaint with summons) and, therefore, the complaint is liable to be rejected. A person who does not pay within 15 days of receipt of the summons from the court along with the copy of complaint U/s 138 of the Act, cannot obviously contend that there was no proper service of notice as required U/s 138, by ignoring statutory presumption to the contrary U/s 27 of the General Clauses Act and Section 114 of the Evidence Act." 24.In view hereof, the legal demand notice Ex. CW1/5 is held to have been duly served upon the Accused. Finally, the complaint has been filed within the limitation period. 25.Finally, the complaint has been filed within the limitation period. Therefore, essential ingredients (i) to (v) as stipulated by the Hon'ble SC in Kusum Ingots Case (supra), have been duly satisfied. 26.Further, as noted above, once the execution of the cheque by the Accused is proved/admitted, the presumption of the same being drawn for consideration stands attracted in terms of Section 139 NI Act. Now, in the case at hand, so far as the question of existence of basic ingredients for drawing of presumption U/s 118 (a) and 139 of the NI Act is concerned, from the aforesaid discussion, it is apparent that the Accused has not denied his signatures on the cheque in question 11 | P a g e CC No. 629035/2016 Delhi Nagrik Sehkari Bank vs Chander Pal that has been drawn in favour of the Complainant on a bank account maintained by the Accused; and hence the said presumption can be drawn. 27.The Ld. Counsel for the Accused has stated that such inference cannot be drawn as the Accused had given the cheque as a blank signed cheque and the particulars on the same have been filled by or at the instance of the Complainant. At this stage, reliance can be laid on the observations of the Hon'ble SC in Bir Singh v. Mukesh Kumar , (2019) 4 SCC 197; wherein it has been held that: "It is immaterial that the cheque may have been filled in by any person other than the drawer, if the cheque is duly signed by the drawer. If the cheque is otherwise valid, the penal provisions of Section 138 would be attracted... 38. If a signed blank cheque is voluntarily presented to a payee, towards some payment, the payee may fill up the amount and other particulars. This in itself would not invalidate the cheque. The onus would still be on the Accused to prove that the cheque was not in discharge of a debt or liability by adducing evidence... 40. Even a blank cheque leaf voluntarily signed and handed over by the Accused, which is towards some payment, would attract presumption Under Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, in the absence of any cogent evidence to show that the cheque was not issued in discharge 12 | P a g e CC No. 629035/2016 Delhi Nagrik Sehkari Bank vs Chander Pal of a debt." (emphasis supplied) 28.The same view has been endorsed by the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in Ravi Chopra v. State, CRL.M.C. 5211/2006; wherein it was observed that: "A collective reading of the above provisions shows that even under the scheme of the NI Act it is possible for the drawer of a cheque to give a blank cheque signed by him to the payee and consent either impliedly or expressly to the said cheque being filled up at a subsequent point in time and presented for payment by the drawee. There is no provision in the NI Act which either defines the difference in the handwriting or the ink pertaining to the material particulars filled up in comparison with the signature thereon as constituting a "material alteration" for the purposes of Section 87 NI Act. What however is essential is that the cheque must have been signed by the drawer." (emphasis supplied) 29.Hence, in view of such clear stipulation by the Hon'ble SC and Hon'ble Delhi High Court, it is immaterial whether the particulars on the cheque have been filled by the Accused or not, to the extent the Accused has admitted to have appended his signatures on the cheque in question. Accordingly, the applicability of the presumption under Section 139 NI Act is not dependent upon the Accused filling the particulars on the cheque. Accordingly, it is required to be presumed 13 | P a g e CC No. 629035/2016 Delhi Nagrik Sehkari Bank vs Chander Pal that the cheque in question was drawn for consideration and the holder of the cheque i.e., the Complainant received the same in discharge of an existing debt. The onus, therefore, shifts on the Accused to establish a probable defence so as to rebut such a presumption. 30.In the segment on legal framework, set out above, the legal proposition with respect to the burden of proof upon the Accused has already been discussed. Hence, it is now to be examined as to whether the Accused brought any material on record or pointed out glaring discrepancies in the material produced by the Complainant for dislodging the presumption which meets the standard of preponderance of probabilities. 31.The Accused in the present case, has taken the following line of defence with a view to rebut the presumption: (A) The cheque in question was issued as a security cheque: 32.The Accused in his defence evidence as well as statement u/s 251 CrPC as well examination u/s 313 CrPC has submitted that the cheque in question was given as a security cheque and not for repayment, and hence, the provisions of Section 138 NI Act do not apply. In this regard, it is noted that the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in Suresh Chandra Goyal v. Amit Singhal, Crl . L.P, 706/2014 has succinctly observed that: " Section 138 of NI Act does not distinguish between a cheque issued by 14 | P a g e CC No. 629035/2016 Delhi Nagrik Sehkari Bank vs Chander Pal the debtor in discharge of an existing debt or other liability, or a cheque issued as a security cheque on the premise that on the due future date the debt which shall have crystallized by then, shall be paid. So long as there is a debt existing, in respect whereof the cheque in question is issued, in my view, the same would attract Section 138 of NI Act in case of its dishonour." 33.Hence, it appears that if on the date of presentment of cheque, liability of the Accused existed towards the Complainant, the same would fall under Section 138 NI Act, even if the same was issued as a security cheque; and hence, it is not relevant if the cheque in question was issued with the intent of being a security cheque. In fact, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in a recent judgment of the Sunil Todi Case (supra), has held that the provisions of Section 138 NI Act apply to cheques issued on advance basis as well, if at the time of presentation of the same, liability exists. It was observed that: "The object of the NI Act is to enhance the acceptability of cheques and inculcate faith in the efficiency of negotiable instruments for transaction of business. The purpose of the provision would become otiose if the provision is interpreted to exclude cases where debt is incurred after the drawing of the cheque but before its encashment. In Indus Airways, advance payments were made but since the purchase agreement was cancelled, there was no occasion of incurring any debt. The true purpose 15 | P a g e CC No. 629035/2016 Delhi Nagrik Sehkari Bank vs Chander Pal of Section 138 would not be fulfilled, if 'debt or other liability' is interpreted to include only a debt that exists as on the date of drawing of the cheque." (emphasis added) 34.Hence, unless it is shown that no liability existed on the date of presentation, either because no loan had already been repaid by other modes or that no loan was taken; provision of Section 138 NI Act would apply to cheques issued on an advance basis as well. Accordingly, this argument/defence of the Accused, by itself, does not rebut the presumption u/s 139 NI Act. (B) Repayment of loan amount: 35.The Accused has not denied the loan taken from the Complainant. In fact, in his defence evidence, he has stated that he was a member of the Complainant bank and that he had taken a loan of Rs. 5 Lakhs from the Complainant on 05.04.2011 which was repayable in 80 installments of Rs. 10,675/- each. He has further stated that the cheque in question was handed over to the bank on 10.08.2015 towards discharge of the loan liability. However, his defence is that he is not liable to pay the cheque amount to the Complainant as he has repaid a substantial amount of loan. It is a matter of record that no cross-examination of the Complainant has been conducted. 36.In support of his defence, the Accused has examined himself and Ms. Vandana Aggarwal, clerk cum cashier at Delhi Nagrik Sehkari Bank as DW-2. DW2 has brought the statement of account of the Accused maintained with the 16 | P a g e CC No. 629035/2016 Delhi Nagrik Sehkari Bank vs Chander Pal Complainant bank, Ex. DW2/X, for the period 05.04.2011 till 01.02.2016; and 15.02.2016 to 30.09.2021. Perusal of Ex. DW2/X shows that as on 21.09.2015, i.e., the date of presentation of the cheque; an amount of Rs. 3,32,425/- was repaid by the Accused and principal amount of Rs. 4,55,308/- remained unpaid, as per the statement of account filed by the Accused, i.e., Ex. DW2/X. The Complainant Bank in their complaint has submitted that the cheque in question was given as part payment of the remaining principal amount. The Accused in his cross-examination dt. 16.11.2019 has further stated that: "It is correct that loan was taken by me at 15% rate of interest and I had also executed loan document in favour of the bank in this regard. As per my memory, I paid the aforesaid installment to the bank on around upto one year. Thereafter, I could not made payment of installment on regular intervals to the bank because of my personal reason." 37. Accordingly, in his cross-examination, the Accused has conceded to his lapse in payment of the installments to the Complainant Bank. He has also in cross- examination dt. 16.11.2019, states that "It is correct that I have not cleared the aforesaid amount till date." Thereby, admitting his liability towards the Complainant. Further, even as per the statement of account summoned by him as part of defence evidence as on 22.09.2015 (i.e., the time of presentment of the cheque); a liability of Rs. 4,55,308/- stood outstanding on him. Further as 17 | P a g e CC No. 629035/2016 Delhi Nagrik Sehkari Bank vs Chander Pal per the cross examination of the Accused; an amount of Rs. 8,54,000/-3 was to be paid to the Complainant Bank in 80 installments; and as per the statement produced by him, an amount of Rs. 3,32,425/- had only been repaid by him; leaving a balance of Rs. 5,21,575/- , being due towards the Complainant Bank. Further, the entries of payment, which are stated to be deductions made from his salary, marked as A-20 to A-38 in Ex. DW2/X are not relevant as the same pertain to the period of 18.12.2018 to 23.06.2020; being payments/deductions made 2/3 years after institution of the complaint. It is trite law that the amount demanded in the legal demand notice is required to be paid by the Accused within 15 days of the receipt thereof, otherwise, the offence under section 138 NI Act stands committed. Subsequent payments/deduction from salary may be relevant at the time of sentencing, but do not obliterate the offence u/s 138 NI Act. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Rajneesh Aggarwal vs. Amit J. Bhalla , 2001 DCR 1, had observed that: "7. So far as the question of deposit of the money during the pendency of these appeals is concerned, we may state that in course of hearing the parties wanted to settle the matter in Court and it is in that connection, to prove the bonafide, the respondent deposited the amount covered under all the three cheques in the Court, but the complainant's counsel insisted that if there is going to be a settlement, then all the pending cases between 3 i.e., the installment of Rs. 10,675 multiplied by 80. 18 | P a g e CC No. 629035/2016 Delhi Nagrik Sehkari Bank vs Chander Pal the parties should be settled, which was, however, not agreed to by the respondent and, therefore, the matter could not be settled. So far as the criminal complaint is concerned, once the offence is committed, any payment made subsequent thereto will not absolve the accused of the liability of criminal offence, though in the matter of awarding of sentence, it may have some effect on the Courts trying the offence. But by no stretch of imagination, a criminal proceeding could be quashed on account of deposit of money in the Court or that an order of quashing of criminal proceeding, which is otherwise unsustainable in law, could be sustained because of the deposit of money in this Court. In this view of the matter, the so-called deposit of money by the respondent in this Court is of no consequence." (emphasis added) 38.Accordingly, the defence of the Accused as to the absence of liability towards the cheque in question due to the repayment of loan amount has not been proved by the standard of preponderance of probabilities; and the evidence produced by him supports the version of the Complainant, as to the fact of existence of liability towards the Complainant to the full extent of the cheque amount; on the date of dishonour of the cheque in question. Conclusion 39.In these circumstances and in view of the above detailed discussion, this court is of the considered opinion that the Accused has not successfully rebutted the 19 | P a g e CC No. 629035/2016 Delhi Nagrik Sehkari Bank vs Chander Pal presumption under Section 139 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 and the ingredients of Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 stand proved. Therefore, Accused Chanderpal is held guilty and is Convicted of the offence punishable under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instrument Act, 1881. ORDER: CONVICTED Announced in Open Court (Twinkle Chawla) 11.03.2022 MM (NI-Act 02), South East Saket Court, New Delhi Note: This judgment contains 20 pages and each page has been signed by me.
